title: Anisotropic hot carrier relaxation mediated by electron phonon scattering in TiN thin films
authors: Hemant Verma, Tzu-Yu Peng, Shyr-Shyan Yeh, Sheng-Chieh Huang, Pritam Sardar, Yang-Hao Chan, Yu-Jung Lu, Chao-Cheng Kaun
abstract: Crystal orientations can shape the ultrafast energy relaxations of transition-metal nitride thin films. Here, we investigate the orientation-dependent electron-phonon (e-ph) mediated relaxation in titanium nitride (TiN) thin films along the [100], [110], and [111] directions by combining first-principles calculations with ultrafast pump-probe transient absorption spectroscopy. Using maximally localized Wannier functions, we evaluate e-ph quasiparticle scattering lifetimes near the Fermi level and identify a clear anisotropy: The TiN [111] orientation exhibits a longer e-ph scattering lifetime (15.96 fs) than [100] (13.69 fs) and [110] (11.12 fs), indicating reduced intrinsic e-ph scattering strength. Furthermore, we grew quasi-epitaxial, orientation-controlled TiN thin films on MgO substrates. Pump-probe measurements reveals that the population-level relaxation (hot-electron cooling) time also depends on orientations, with [111] films showing a significantly slower decay (110 fs) than [100] (90 fs) and [110] (80 fs). We emphasize that the calculated few-femtosecond scattering lifetimes and the measured few-hundred-femtosecond cooling time respectively represent single-event scattering and collective cooling, yet they exhibit consistent trends. These results demonstrate that crystallographic orientation provides a practical and powerful route to tune e-ph-governed relaxation in TiN thin films, offering essential design guidelines for refractory plasmonic and energy-conversion platforms.
summary: This work demonstrates that the crystal orientation of TiN thin films critically controls how fast hot carriers cool down via electron-phonon scattering. By combining first-principles theory and pump-probe measurements, the authors show that the [111] direction exhibits a significantly slower relaxation rate compared to other orientations. This finding provides crucial guidelines for engineering energy conversion devices using anisotropic materials.
main_problem: The study investigates how crystallographic orientation dictates the rate of hot carrier energy relaxation mediated by electron-phonon (e-ph) scattering in TiN thin films.
main_result: Both theoretical calculations and ultrafast spectroscopy show that the [111] orientation leads to a slower decay/longer lifetime compared to the [100] and [110] directions, demonstrating strong crystallographic control over energy dissipation.
method: The research combines first-principles DFT calculations using MLWFs (for theoretical scattering lifetimes) with ultrafast pump-probe transient absorption spectroscopy (TAS) measurements (for experimental cooling times).
model_or_system: The system is quasi-epitaxial Titanium Nitride (TiN) thin films grown on MgO substrates, analyzed along the [100], [110], and [111] crystal axes.
key_observables: Electron-phonon scattering lifetime ($\tau_{\text{e-ph}}$) and population-level hot-electron cooling time ($\tau_{\text{cooling}}$).
important_parameters: Crystallographic orientation ([100], [110], [111]), temperature (room temperature), and characteristic timescales (few-fs to hundreds-of-fs).
main_assumptions: The calculated lifetimes represent single-event scattering, while measured times reflect collective cooling dynamics; however, the trends are consistent.
figures_summary: Figures likely show optimized slab structures, electronic band diagrams, and time-resolved TAS kinetics plots comparing the three orientations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of anisotropic relaxation, presents theoretical calculations based on first principles to predict scattering rates for different crystal faces, validates these predictions against experimental TAS measurements, and concludes by emphasizing orientation control as a design tool.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter physics (plasmonics/energy conversion), the study models non-equilibrium energy transport dynamics using ultrafast spectroscopy and quantum calculations, which shares methodological overlap with open quantum systems modeling of energy relaxation.
